title: Three Men Refuse to Bow
overview: When King Nebuchadnezzar orders everyone to worship a giant gold statue, three Jewish officials refuse, are thrown into a furnace, and walk out unharmed.

parts.label: The gold statue (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: The statue was about 27 metres (90 feet) tall and was probably covered in gold rather than solid, and bowing to it was a public test of loyalty to the king and his empire. It is unclear whether it stood for one of Babylon's gods or for the king himself.

parts.label: The three are reported (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego are the Babylonian names given to three young Jewish exiles who held high posts in the province. Their accusers may have been jealous rivals, and they stress that the men reject not only the statue but all the king's gods.

parts.label: Rescue or no rescue (vv. 13-18)
parts.note: The king gives them a second chance and mocks the idea that any god could save them. They answer that their God can rescue them, but whether he does or not, they still will not bow, so their loyalty does not depend on being saved.

parts.label: Into the furnace (vv. 19-23)
parts.note: The king orders the furnace heated far beyond normal, meaning as hot as it could possibly be made, and the fire is so fierce that it kills the soldiers who throw the men in. Some ancient translations add a long prayer and song here that are not in the original Aramaic text.

parts.label: A fourth figure (vv. 24-27)
parts.note: The king sees the three walking free inside the fire with a fourth figure who looks divine, and when they come out not even their clothes smell of smoke. The king himself calls this figure an angel, though many Christians have read it as an appearance of Christ.

parts.label: The king's turnaround (vv. 28-30)
parts.note: Nebuchadnezzar praises their God and promotes the three men. Yet his new decree is itself a violent threat, which suggests he now honours this God as powerful without giving up his own gods or his harsh rule.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the story is straightforward history or a story told to strengthen Jews facing later persecution, and on whether the fourth figure in the fire was an angel or Christ appearing before his birth.
think: Is there anything you would refuse to do even if refusing cost you dearly and no rescue came?
